title: How Bioarchaeology Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore bioarchaeology, a field that combines archaeology with scientific techniques (DNA analysis, mass spectrometry, isotope analysis) to read bones, teeth, and feces for information about individual lives and whole societies. They cover Jane Ellen Buikstra's 1977 definition, the shift from "great man" historiography to history from below, Neanderthal coprolites showing plant eating, copro-archaeology and preserved fecal samples, strontium isotopes marking childhood origins, stable isotope diet analysis, the Beauty of Xiaohe mummies from the Taklamakan Desert, DNA and cemetery kinship studies, repatriation and cultural patrimony laws (UNESCO 1970, NAGPRA), the Salvador Dali exhumation paternity claim, and why the field matters for questions about violence and climate change. The episode ends with listener mail about the four-way stop wave.

segments.title: Introduction to bioarchaeology
segments.summary: Hosts introduce archaeology and the Indiana Jones image, then describe bioarchaeology as a technique-driven subfield that applies science like genetics and mass spectrometry to bones, and aims at broader social history.

segments.title: Definition and history of the term bioarchaeology
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh trace the term to British archaeologist Sir John Graham Douglas Clark and to American anthropologist Jane Ellen Buikstra, who in 1977 defined it as integrating archaeology and human osteology to investigate biocultural change.

segments.title: Bones as material culture and the 2017 WWII couple found in Alps
segments.summary: Hosts note that bones and teeth are the most durable evidence and that skeletons record life experiences such as violence and disease. They briefly mention a World War Two couple found frozen in the Swiss Alps.

segments.title: Neanderthal coprolites and fecal analysis
segments.summary: Discussion of Neanderthal fossil feces showing a plant-rich diet of berries, nuts and tubers, which challenges the idea that they ate mostly meat, and how this bears on the megafauna extinction debate. The hosts also cover the history of coprolite study and how it is now preserved for later analysis.

segments.title: Coprolite evidence of cannibalism and Richard III
segments.summary: Hosts describe protein evidence of cannibalism found in ancient feces from southwestern groups, linked to climate-driven starvation, and mention Pierce Mitchell's finding that Richard III had roundworm.

segments.title: Teeth, strontium isotopes and stable isotope diet analysis
segments.summary: Teeth show childhood malnutrition lines. Strontium isotopes in teeth reflect childhood region of origin, while bone isotopes reflect later life, revealing migration. Stable carbon and nitrogen isotope ratios indicate diet such as meat, maize or wheat.

segments.title: Beauty of Xiaohe mummies and burial goods
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the well-preserved mummies from the Xiaohe district of the Taklamakan Desert in western China, about four thousand years old, buried with felt hats and boots, some with red hair and European features, possibly a pastoral group from western Europe. Burial goods and treatment after death are said to reveal social values.

segments.title: Ancient DNA, kinship and social hierarchy in cemeteries
segments.summary: Ancient DNA can establish sex, relatedness, and marriage patterns. Cemetery analysis combining DNA, diet and bone density can test assumptions about social hierarchy and labor.

segments.title: Repatriation, cultural patrimony and ethics of excavation
segments.summary: Excavating graves raises controversy. UNESCO's 1970 convention and the US NAGPRA law address illicit trade and tribal ownership of cultural patrimony. The hosts discuss the history of collecting remains and the importance of working with local indigenous communities.

segments.title: Salvador Dali exhumation paternity claim
segments.summary: Brief news item: officials in Spain are exhuming Salvador Dali to test whether fortune teller Pilar Abel is his daughter; the Dali Foundation opposes it, and the hosts discuss the ethics and the estate stakes.

segments.title: Why bioarchaeology matters
segments.summary: Hosts conclude that the field helps reconstruct common people's history, tests whether humans are inherently violent, and shows how past societies responded to climate change.

segments.title: Listener mail: the four-way stop wave
segments.summary: Listener Michaela asks whether waving others through a four-way stop is controlling, as her boyfriend suggests. The hosts share their own habits and etiquette views.

segments.title: Outro and contact information
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and give social media and email contact details.
